item.title: 🔴 Thousands of GitHub repos hit with secret-stealing malware
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Researchers have uncovered a campaign in which hijacked GitHub accounts spread secret-stealing malware across thousands of repositories. The payload executed in at least 1,806 repos, exfiltrating CI/CD secrets and cloud credentials.

Aikido Security, which detected and documented the campaign, said the attackers used the 4,837 compromised accounts to open probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories starting Nov. 10. Around 92% of those pull requests, titled “docs: dependency audit notes,” are still open, which suggests most project owners have not seen them.

However, the probes on their own are benign and were performed only to check whether the hijacked accounts had write-access in those repos so that the attackers could follow up with commits that contained the malicious payload: a 1,500-line shell script that collects GitHub Actions secrets, cloud credentials, and API keys for AI services and developer tools.

item.title: 🔴 How AI is changing the nature of cyberattacks
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

AI may be helping cyberattackers increase the speed and scale of their operations, but it is not yet changing their core objectives or the techniques they employ as part of their attack chains.

Phishing, malware, and vulnerability exploitation remain the main techniques in play even as abuse of AI tools has made attacks easier to mount and cheaper for even relatively unskilled attackers, according to security experts.

“Attackers are still identifying targets, performing reconnaissance, establishing a foothold, moving laterally, achieving their objective, covering their tracks, and moving on to the next target,” says Ronald Lewis, director of cybersecurity governance at application security firm Black Duck. “What’s changed is the volume and velocity that AI allows this process to happen.”

item.title: 🟠 An AI kill switch isn’t enough. Build a fallback plan
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

On the morning of Sept. 3, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok all went down within a few hours of one another. OpenAI blamed a routing error, Anthropic cited an infrastructure issue and xAI gave no cause. Service was back by early afternoon, and most of the coverage focused on people who couldn’t write, code or research for a morning.

I read it differently. The question that matters for a security leader isn’t which provider failed. It’s how many workflows in your company had somewhere else to go when it did.

Two months earlier, we saw the opposite failure. Instead of AI that stopped when nobody wanted it to, it was AI that kept going when everybody wanted it stopped. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 is reporting today that it has tracked a massive China-based attack leveraging the open-source AI penetration testing framework Cairn to autonomously conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. The attackers weaponized Cairn by pairing it with Chinese AI models Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek, Unit 42 said.

The report said it monitored the attacks in August and September 2026 in which the Chinese-speaking attackers were able to successfully achieve unauthorized access at 10 of the targeted businesses, accessing dozens of valid credentials. It captured more than one million records at one business, grabbed military and government identities at others, created persistent admin accounts in multiple product systems.

item.title: 🔴 Hackers abuse SQL Server’s weak passwords to drop cryptominers and Gh0st RAT
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

An active threat campaign is combining port scanning, password guessing, and Transact-SQL (T-SQL) commands to compromise exposed Microsoft SQL servers and deliver malware.

The attackers are using predefined username and password lists to brute-force into these servers and exploit their administrative capabilities to execute commands on the underlying Windows systems.

The activity highlights the persistent challenge of securing privileged access across complex and often legacy infrastructure, said Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security. “While internet-facing databases are sometimes the unintended result of technical debt or misconfigurations, relying on static, standing credentials is what turns that exposure into a critical vulnerability,” he said. “When administrative logins can be brute-forced, attackers gain immediate, unchecked control to deploy malware without needing a single complex exploit.”

item.title: 🟠 AI found Linux kernel bugs that remained undetected for decades
item.description:
Why this matters: Privilege-escalation risk — review local admin and endpoint controls.

A Microsoft research project combining AI agents with human security researchers uncovered 59 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, including bugs that had survived in production code for more than 20 years.

While AI dramatically accelerated the discovery process, the researchers found that validating flaws, developing patches, and working with maintainers remained overwhelmingly human-intensive.

The research, conducted by Microsoft’s FORGE Lab under the codename MDASH, generated 26,502 potential findings in approximately two weeks of scanning selected Linux kernel subsystems. Automated screening, proof-of-concept testing, and human validation narrowed these down to 59 public upstream reports, Microsoft said in a blog post.

“We developed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, and fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into mainline,” the researchers said in the blog post.…

item.title: 🟠 The developer laptop just became production. Now what?
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

For decades, enterprise software development relied on an assumption that developers could experiment relatively safely because there were safeguards between their work and production. Development, staging and production had different rules, with human intermediaries making judgments about what was ready to move forward. Testing also assumed that software would behave predictably when executed again.

Coding agents are upending both assumptions. Developers now run autonomous software on laptops containing GitHub tokens, SSH keys, cloud credentials and authenticated browser sessions. They’re connecting agents to MCP servers, granting access to repositories and services, and copying suggested commands into terminals without always understanding what those commands will do. When permission prompts become an obstacle, it’s tempting to click through them or enable unrestricted access. Developers are inventing security policies on the fly.

The result is that the developer laptop has become an extension of production. An agent…

item.title: 🔵 Rewriting less than 10 neurons in an LLM can turn it into a sleeper backdoor
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

Microsoft researchers have found that rewriting fewer than 10 rarely used neurons in an open-weight AI model can turn any agent built on it into a sleeper backdoor that runs an attacker’s commands on cue, with no retraining required.

Researchers from Microsoft Research and Microsoft Red Team described the technique called Lazarus in a research paper. It modifies dormant neurons in a model’s final feed-forward layer to recognize a trigger and inject attacker-controlled commands into the model’s output. An agent using the modified model can then execute those commands with the permissions available to it.

item.title: 🔵 Claude Code’s ‘don’t ask again’ button has a secrets-spilling problem
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

A configuration file meant to store local command permissions on Anthropic’s Claude Code is exposing thousands of API keys, database credentials and other secrets, according to findings by GitGuardian.

The code security firm identified 31,088 distinct secrets in Claude Code’s “.claude/settings.local.json” files across 23,276 public GitHub repositories. Of those, 5343 were still valid when GitGuardian detected them. The exposed credentials include database connection strings, cloud provider tokens, SSH passwords, Google API keys, and AU service credentials.

“Monthly leaks in settings.local.json peaked at 12,535 occurrences in April 2026, then fell to 959 by October, and we do not yet know what changed,” GitGuardian researcher Guillaume Valadon said in a blog post.

item.title: 🔴 Why does old access outlive the job?
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Old access persists beyond its intended purpose and most organizations never monitor it. New access rights arrive within a day of a request. Old rights get revoked, if they get revoked at all, only upon prompting someone. Tools that assist employees in confirming, rotating and vaulting their service accounts have taught me again and again that removing access has to be as thoughtful as granting access. Security professionals can bridge this chasm with simple changes to their policies for role moves and access reviews.

This happens all the time. An employee moves from one team to another. The new manager approves the access needed for the new role within a day, and the person is productive by lunch. The access from the old role stays. After months, access review has one query only: “Do you still need it?” The reviewer sees the name next to the entitlement, but nothing on the dashboard shows whether it has been used since the move. It is hard to click no, because something might get broken. They have never been bothered to click yes. Thus, they click yes, and it’s fine by them.

item.description:

Just over a year ago, before advanced AI models began discovering software vulnerabilities at a nearly unmanageable scale in the so-called vulnpocalypse, three industry experts pioneered the concept of “VulnOps.”

VulnOps, as envisioned by Heather Adkins, Gadi Evron, and Bruce Schneier, is a significant phase in the evolution of AI-assisted cyber defense in which vulnerability research and remediation would become scalable, repeatable, automated, and integrated into enterprise operations. They contemplated that this new era of organizational vulnerability management would progress from AI-augmented vulnerability management to self-healing networks.

item.description:
Why this matters: Advanced threat activity — review privileged access, persistence detection, and lateral-movement controls.

There’s a new flavor of cereal on the table, but not the appealing kind, particularly for defenders.

A new report from global security company ESET describes a “sophisticated, modular, and tightly interconnected” toolset designed to run on compromised Exchange servers for long-term cyberespionage.

The malware is named ‘Cereal’ because it relies heavily on serialization, a technique used to package data and code for transport. It comprises a novel Exchange email collection module, a sneaky command and control (C&C) mechanism, and clever .NET execution tricks.

While as of now, it is being used by nation-state actors to attack government bodies, enterprises should still be concerned.

item.title: 🟠 Commvault rolls out an automated recovery mechanism, promising faster restoration of business
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

Commvault on Tuesday rolled out its answer to enterprise backup restoration nightmares. Called Recovery Studio, the vendor promised that the product would “orchestrate the recovery of applications, identities, configurations, infrastructure dependencies, and datasets together in an automated, runbook-driven workflow.”

Analysts and consultants applauded the effort, agreeing that enterprises today struggle with fast, accurate and secure restorations. But they also stressed that the new system, which is targeted for early access in December with general availability “in the coming months,” places the onus on IT to keep a dependency map current. 

Recovery Studio isn’t using any form of AI to figure out proper restoration details. It relies on a map of assets, dependencies, and other relevant information that the customer creates and maintains, and for many enterprises, the challenge of keeping such a document current is the real problem. Even discounting the times when a line of business doesn’t tell IT about an application change, IT teams struggle to keep up with the speed of change in th…

item.title: 🟠 Finite State Raises $27 Million to Help Device Makers Fight ‘Vulnpocalypse’ with AI-Powered Product Security
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

Funding Will Scale Finite State’s Autonomous Platform and International Expansion as Manufacturers Face a Surge of AI-Discovered Flaws and New Global Security Mandates

Finite State, a leader in product security and software supply chain risk management, today announced a $27 million Series C funding round led by private funds managed by The O.H.I.O. Fund, with participation from CIBC Innovation Banking, Energy Impact Partners, Energize Capital, and National Grid Partners to continue its mission to secure the world’s connected devices.

Finite State’s AI-driven product security platform analyzes the software and firmware inside finished devices, giving manufacturers visibility into the products they build and sell, from vehicles and medical devices to industrial equipment, consumer electronics and critical utility infrastructure. The platform uncovers both known and zero-day vulnerabilities and guides manufacturers in fixing the exploitable ones before attackers strike, making everyday life safer and more secure.

item.description:

A currently exploited zero-day vulnerability that can let attackers steal hashed Outlook NTLM credentials is among the 1,094 holes Microsoft fixed in its November Patch Tuesday releases.

Although rated as only moderate in severity, with a CVSS score of 6.5, Windows administrators need to address CVE-2026-124194 immediately because threat actors are already attacking it. “Don’t let the low score fool you,” said Nick Carroll, cyber incident response manager at Nightwing.

Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024. However, since the user has to open a malicious Office file to launch the attack, good employee cybersecurity awareness training and an effective email gateway could mitigate this attack until the patch is installed.

item.description:

N-able has taken its hosted N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform offline worldwide and shipped an emergency hotfix after a security researcher released 33 zero-day exploits for the software, including attack chains that could let unauthenticated attackers take over servers.

N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to remotely manage, patch, and support endpoint systems, so a compromised server can expose every computer under its control. N-able said it took the hosted environments offline as a precaution and advised customers using the on-premises version to shut down their servers until it released the fix, N-central 2026.4 HF2, on Tuesday.

item.title: 🟠 Microsoft’s AI bug hunter finds Rust flaw that went undetected for nearly 11 years
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

Microsoft researchers have uncovered a memory-safety bug in Rust’s standard library that had gone undetected for nearly 11 years, alongside other flaws that can trigger undefined behavior even in applications written entirely in safe Rust. Two of the findings affect stable Rust, including a separate issue that could cause applications to access freed memory.

The nearly 11-year-old bug involves Rust’s process::exit function. Microsoft’s FORGE Lab researchers found that calling the function from a child thread could cause the runtime to remove the main thread’s alternate signal stack while it was still running. If the main thread subsequently experienced a stack overflow, the operating system could be unable to deliver the signal correctly, resulting in a segmentation fault instead of Rust’s intended stack-overflow handling.

item.description:

An attacker has abused AWS cross-account IAM roles to access multiple customer environments, steal data, and harvest credentials in a supply-chain attack that ran between October 14 and October 26.

Researchers from Wiz, working with Sentra and Mandiant, said they observed an attacker using IAM credentials for Qubole’s AWS account to assume roles in customer environments.

The compromised credentials allowed the attacker to access customer AWS accounts that had previously established cross-account access permissions with Qubole. The access was used to enumerate cloud resources, retrieve secrets and configuration data, download files from Amazon S3, and test credentials belonging to affected organizations.

item.title: 🔵 Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
item.description:
Why this matters: Regulatory/compliance context — assess scope and action timeline.
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

item.title: 🔵 Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
item.description:
Why this matters: Regulatory/compliance context — assess scope and action timeline.
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user's Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet's access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
